results.title: Deciding within a time bound
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A code $c$ decides a decision problem $L$ within the time bound $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ when, on every bit list $x$, the machine of $c$ started on the input word of $x$ halts within $t(|x|)$ steps, and its tape from the head rightwards, without trailing blanks, is the single symbol of the answer $L(x)$: $2$ for true and $1$ for false.

results.title: Time classes on codes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $\mathrm{CodeTime}(t)$ is the class of decision problems $L$ such that some code decides $L$ within $t(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$.

results.title: Deciding within a larger time bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a code $c$ decides a decision problem $L$ within a time bound $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, and $t' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfies $t(n) \le t'(n)$ for every $n$, then $c$ decides $L$ within $t'$.

results.title: Monotonicity of time classes on codes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t, t' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $t(n) \le t'(n)$ for every $n$. Then every decision problem that some code decides within $t(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$ is decided by some code within $t'(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$: $\mathrm{CodeTime}(t) \subseteq \mathrm{CodeTime}(t')$.

results.title: The constant-false code
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The code whose table has a single row, for state $0$: on the blank $0$ it writes the symbol $1$, the symbol of the bit false, and enters state $1$; on the input symbols $1$ and $2$ it moves right and stays in state $0$; on every other symbol it halts. State $1$ has no row, so the machine halts there. This code answers false on every input.

results.title: The constant-false code decides the empty language
results.caption: Theorem

Then $c$ decides the empty language within $n + 1$ steps on every input of length $n$.

results.title: Time classes are not empty once the bound exceeds the input length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $n + 1 \le f(n)$ for every $n$. Then the empty language, the decision problem that answers false on every bit list, belongs to the time class of $f$: some code decides it within $f(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$, where $|x|$ is the length of $x$.

results.summary: For $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the diagonal language of $f$ holds at a bit list $x$ iff $x$ encodes a code $c$ and the clocked evaluator, running $c$ on $x$ for at most $f(|x|)$ steps, does not return the output $[2]$, the symbol of the answer true: either $c$ does not halt on $x$ within $f(|x|)$ steps, or it halts with another output. results.title: Decoding inverts the code stack
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit list $x$ and every code $c$, if $x$ decodes to $c$, then the code stack of $c$ is $x$.

results.title: Code stacks are recognized
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit list $x$, the decoding of $x$ as a code succeeds iff $x$ is the code stack of some code.

results.title: Code stacks, entry by entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A bit list $x$ encodes a code (its decoding succeeds) iff there is a list of entries $(q, a, q', s)$ of natural numbers whose keys $(q, a)$ strictly increase in lexicographic order, such that $x$ is the list of cells of the numbers of these entries, four numbers per entry.

results.title: Code stacks decode to codes with the same code stack
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every code $c$, decoding the code stack of $c$ succeeds and returns a code $c'$ whose code stack equals the code stack of $c$.

results.title: The diagonal language on a code stack
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every time bound $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every code $c$ with code stack $x$, the bit list $x$ belongs to the diagonal language for $f$ iff it is not the case that $c$, run on $x$, halts within $f(|x|)$ steps with output the single symbol $2$ of the bit true.

results.title: Bit lists that encode no code are outside the diagonal language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every bit list $x$ that is the code stack of no code, $x$ is not in the diagonal language of $f$.

results.title: The diagonal language through the universal machine
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every time bound $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every code $c$ with code stack $x$, the bit list $x$ belongs to the diagonal language for $f$ iff the output encoding of the result of running $c$ on $x$ for at most $f(|x|)$ steps differs from the output encoding of the result whose output is the single symbol $2$ of the bit true.

results.title: The diagonal argument
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the diagonal language of $f$ is not in the time class of $f$ on codes: no code decides it on every input $x$ within $f(|x|)$ steps. This is the argument from the proof of Sipser's Theorem 9.10: a code $c$ deciding it would, on its own code stack, answer the opposite of the diagonal language of $f$.

results.title: A hierarchy within codes, given an upper bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f, g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $f(n) \le g(n)$ for every $n$, and for a time bound $t$ let $\mathrm{CodeTime}(t)$ be the class of decision problems that some code decides within $t(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$. If the diagonal language $\mathrm{diag}(f)$ belongs to $\mathrm{CodeTime}(g)$, then $\mathrm{CodeTime}(f)$ is a proper subclass of $\mathrm{CodeTime}(g)$.

results.title: The universal machine's argument for the diagonal language
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a time bound $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a bit list $x$, the argument is a triple of a code, an input and a clock. If $x$ decodes to a code $c$, it is $(c, x, f(|x|))$. Otherwise it is the code with the empty table, the input consisting of the single bit true, and the clock $0$; that code halts at once with the answer true, so that the diagonal answer is false there.

results.title: The diagonal answer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a clocked result $o$, either a timeout or the output of a halted run, the diagonal answer of $o$ is false if $o$ is the output consisting of the single symbol $2$, the symbol of the bit true, and true otherwise, including on a timeout.

results.title: The diagonal answer read from the encoded output
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every clocked result $o$, either a timeout or the output of a halted run, the diagonal answer of $o$ is true exactly when the output encoding of $o$ differs from the output encoding of the result whose output is the single symbol $2$ of the bit true, which is the bit list true, true, true, false.

results.title: The diagonal language through the clocked evaluator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every bit list $x$, let $(c, y, T)$ be the universal machine's argument for the diagonal language of $f$ on $x$. Then the diagonal language of $f$ holds at $x$ iff the clocked evaluator, running $c$ on $y$ for at most $T$ steps, does not return the output $[2]$, the symbol of the answer true.

results.title: The quadratic diagonal language is in P

results.title: Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem

results.title: Directed adjacency graph
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A directed adjacency graph on a type $V$ consists of a list of vertices that has no duplicates and contains every element of $V$ (so $V$ is finite), together with, for each vertex $v$, an ordered list of the out-neighbors of $v$, in which entries may repeat.

results.title: Edge of a directed adjacency graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ on $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, there is an edge from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ when $t$ occurs in the adjacency list of $s$.

results.title: Walks of a given length
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$, a natural number $n$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ when there are vertices $v_0, \dots, v_n$ with $v_0 = s$ and $v_n = t$ such that $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ is an edge of $G$ for every $i < n$.

results.title: The digraph of a directed adjacency graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The digraph associated with a directed adjacency graph $G$ on a vertex type $V$ is the directed graph on $V$ in which $s$ is adjacent to $t$ exactly when $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$. It forgets the order of the adjacency lists and the multiplicity of their entries.

results.title: Adjacency in the associated digraph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, $s$ is adjacent to $t$ in the digraph associated with $G$ if and only if $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$, that is, $t$ occurs in the adjacency list of $s$.

results.title: Walks of length zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a directed adjacency graph, there is a walk of length $0$ from a vertex $s$ to a vertex $t$ if and only if $s = t$.

results.title: Splitting off the first edge of a walk
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, for every natural number $n$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n + 1$ from $s$ to $t$ if and only if there is a vertex $v$ such that $(s, v)$ is an edge of $G$ and there is a walk of length $n$ from $v$ to $t$.

results.title: Concatenation of walks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on $V$ and let $s, m, t \in V$. If $G$ has a walk of length exactly $a$ from $s$ to $m$ and a walk of length exactly $b$ from $m$ to $t$, then $G$ has a walk of length exactly $a + b$ from $s$ to $t$.

results.title: Reachability in a directed graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, $t$ is reachable from $s$ when the pair $(s, t)$ lies in the reflexive-transitive closure of the edge relation of $G$: either $s = t$, or a finite sequence of edges of $G$ leads from $s$ to $t$.

results.title: Reachability by walks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, a vertex $t$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ if and only if there is a natural number $n$ such that $G$ has a walk of length exactly $n$ from $s$ to $t$.

results.title: Reachability is the reflexive-transitive closure of the edge relation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, a vertex $t$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ if and only if $(s, t)$ lies in the reflexive-transitive closure of the edge relation of $G$.

results.title: The transition system of a directed adjacency graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The labelled transition system of a directed adjacency graph $G$ has the vertices of $G$ as states and a single label, and it has a transition from $s$ to $t$ exactly when $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$.

results.title: Reachability in the associated transition system
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, a vertex $t$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ if and only if, in the unit-labelled labelled transition system of $G$, there is a finite list of labels along which $s$ reaches $t$ by a multistep transition.

results.title: Transpose of a directed adjacency graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ on a vertex type with decidable equality, the transpose of $G$ has the same vertex enumeration as $G$, and the adjacency list of a vertex $v$ consists of the vertices $u$ such that $v$ occurs in the adjacency list of $u$ in $G$, each listed once and in the order of the vertex enumeration.

results.title: Edges of the transpose graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ have decidable equality and let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on $V$. For all $s, t \in V$, the transpose of $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$ if and only if $G$ has an edge from $t$ to $s$.

results.title: Walks in the transpose are reversed walks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a directed adjacency graph $G$ on a vertex type with decidable equality, every natural number $n$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in the transpose of $G$ if and only if there is a walk of length $n$ from $t$ to $s$ in $G$.

results.title: Reachability in the transpose graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on a vertex type with decidable equality, and let $G^{\mathsf{T}}$ be its transpose. For all vertices $s$ and $t$, $t$ is reachable from $s$ in $G^{\mathsf{T}}$ if and only if $s$ is reachable from $t$ in $G$.

results.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two directed adjacency graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on the same vertex type are semantically equivalent when they have the same edges: for all vertices $s$ and $t$, $G_1$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$ if and only if $G_2$ does.

results.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs is reflexive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every directed adjacency graph $G$ is semantically equivalent to itself.

results.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs is symmetric
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a directed adjacency graph $G_1$ is semantically equivalent to a directed adjacency graph $G_2$, then $G_2$ is semantically equivalent to $G_1$.

results.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs is transitive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a directed adjacency graph $G_1$ is semantically equivalent to $G_2$, and $G_2$ is semantically equivalent to $G_3$, then $G_1$ is semantically equivalent to $G_3$.

results.title: Semantically equivalent graphs have the same walks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If two directed adjacency graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ are semantically equivalent, then for every natural number $n$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G_1$ if and only if there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G_2$.

results.title: Semantically equivalent graphs have the same reachability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If two directed adjacency graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on $V$ are semantically equivalent, then for all $s, t \in V$, $t$ is reachable from $s$ in $G_1$ if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in $G_2$.

results.title: Transposition preserves semantic equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For directed adjacency graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on a vertex type with decidable equality, if $G_1$ and $G_2$ are semantically equivalent, then their transposes are semantically equivalent.

results.title: Transposing twice gives a semantically equivalent graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on a vertex type with decidable equality. The transpose of the transpose of $G$ is semantically equivalent to $G$, that is, it has exactly the same edges as $G$.

results.title: Boolean edge test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a type $V$ with decidable equality, a directed adjacency graph $G$ on $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, the edge test of $G$ at $(s, t)$ is the Boolean value that is true exactly when $t$ occurs in the adjacency list of $s$.

results.title: The Boolean edge test is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a type $V$ with decidable equality, a directed adjacency graph $G$ on $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, the Boolean edge test of $G$ at $(s, t)$ returns true if and only if $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$.

results.title: Erasing a directed edge
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, erasing the edge $s \to t$ gives the directed-adjacency graph with the same vertex enumeration as $G$ whose out-neighbour list at $s$ is the out-neighbour list of $s$ in $G$ with every occurrence of $t$ removed (the remaining entries keep their order), and whose out-neighbour list at every other vertex is the same as in $G$.

results.title: Erasing an edge keeps the vertex enumeration
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ has the same vertex enumeration as $G$: the same list of vertices, in the same order.

results.title: Out-neighbours of the source after erasing an edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, the out-neighbour list of $s$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ is the out-neighbour list of $s$ in $G$ with every occurrence of $t$ removed, the remaining entries kept in their original order.

results.title: Erasing an edge leaves the other out-neighbour lists unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$, $t$ and $u$ with $u \ne s$, the out-neighbour list of $u$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ equals the out-neighbour list of $u$ in $G$.

results.title: Edges after erasing an edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$, $t$, $u$ and $v$, there is an edge from $u$ to $v$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ if and only if there is an edge from $u$ to $v$ in $G$ and it is not the case that both $u = s$ and $v = t$.

results.title: The erased edge is absent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, the Boolean edge lookup for $s \to t$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ returns false.

results.title: Erasing an edge twice gives the same out-neighbour lists
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, erasing the edge $s \to t$ from $G$ and then erasing it again gives, at every vertex, the same out-neighbour list as erasing it once.

results.title: Walks after erasing an edge are walks in the original graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$, vertices $s$, $t$, $u$ and $v$, and natural number $n$, if there is a walk of length $n$ from $u$ to $v$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$, then there is a walk of length $n$ from $u$ to $v$ in $G$.

results.title: Reachability after erasing an edge implies reachability in the original graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$, $t$, $u$ and $v$, if $v$ is reachable from $u$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$, then $v$ is reachable from $u$ in $G$.

results.title: Tuple
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a type $A$ of attributes and a type $D$ of values, a tuple is a partial assignment of values to attributes: a function that assigns to each attribute $a \in A$ either a value in $D$ or no value, in which case the tuple is undefined at $a$.

results.title: Tuple over a schema
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A tuple $t$ is over the schema $S$, a finite set of attributes, when $t$ is defined exactly on the attributes of $S$: for every attribute $a$, the value $t(a)$ is defined if and only if $a \in S$.

results.title: Compatible tuples
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two tuples $t$ and $u$ are compatible (joinable) when they agree on every attribute where both are defined: for every attribute $a$, either $t$ is undefined at $a$, or $u$ is undefined at $a$, or $t(a) = u(a)$.

results.title: Merge of two tuples
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The merge of tuples $t$ and $u$ is the tuple whose value at each attribute $a$ is $t(a)$ if $t$ is defined at $a$, and $u(a)$ otherwise; it is undefined at $a$ when neither $t$ nor $u$ is.

results.title: Compatibility with a merge, grouped from the left
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For tuples $t$, $u$, $v$: $t$ and $u$ are compatible and the merge of $t$ and $u$ is compatible with $v$ if and only if $t$, $u$, $v$ are pairwise compatible, that is, $t$ and $u$, $t$ and $v$, and $u$ and $v$ are compatible.

results.title: Compatibility with a merge, grouped from the right
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For tuples $t$, $u$, $v$: $u$ and $v$ are compatible and $t$ is compatible with the merge of $u$ and $v$ if and only if $t$, $u$, $v$ are pairwise compatible, that is, $t$ and $u$, $t$ and $v$, and $u$ and $v$ are compatible.

results.title: Restriction of a tuple
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite set $T$ of attributes and a tuple $t$, the restriction $t|_T$ is the tuple that agrees with $t$ on every attribute in $T$ and is undefined on every attribute outside $T$.

results.title: Selection conditions
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The selection conditions over attributes $A$ and values $D$ are generated by: the condition that always holds; the equality $a = c$ of an attribute $a$ with a constant $c \in D$; the equality $a = b$ of two attributes $a$ and $b$; the negation of a condition; and the conjunction of two conditions.

results.title: Truth value of a selection condition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The truth value of a selection condition on a tuple $t$ is defined by recursion: the always-true condition holds; $a = c$ holds when $t$ is defined at $a$ with value $c$; $a = b$ holds when $t(a) = t(b)$ as possibly undefined values, so it also holds when $t$ is undefined at both $a$ and $b$; a negation holds when the negated condition fails; and a conjunction holds when both conditions hold.

results.title: Attributes of a selection condition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The set of attributes mentioned by a selection condition, defined by recursion: it is empty for the always-true condition; for the comparison $a = d$ of an attribute $a$ with a constant $d$ it is $\{a\}$; for the comparison $a = b$ of attributes $a$ and $b$ it is $\{a, b\}$; for the negation $\neg \varphi$ of a condition $\varphi$ it is the set of attributes of $\varphi$; and for the conjunction…

results.title: Selection conditions depend only on their attributes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a selection condition, $t$ a tuple and $T$ a finite set of attributes containing every attribute of $c$. Then $c$ has the same truth value on the restriction of $t$ to $T$ as on $t$.

results.title: Relation over a schema
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A finite set $r$ of tuples is a relation over the schema $S$, a finite set of attributes, when every tuple $t \in r$ is over $S$, that is, $t$ is defined exactly on the attributes of $S$.

results.title: Selection
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a selection condition $c$ and a finite set $r$ of tuples, the selection $\sigma_c(r)$ is the set of tuples $t \in r$ on which $c$ evaluates to true.

results.title: Cascade of selections
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $\sigma_c$ for selection by a selection condition $c$. For selection conditions $c$ and $c'$ and a finite set $r$ of tuples, $\sigma_c(\sigma_{c'}(r)) = \sigma_{c' \land c}(r)$: selecting by $c'$ and then by $c$ is the same as selecting once by the conjunction $c' \land c$.

results.title: Selections commute
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all selection conditions $c$ and $c'$ and every finite set $r$ of tuples, selecting by $c'$ and then by $c$ gives the same result as selecting by $c$ and then by $c'$: $\sigma_c(\sigma_{c'}(r)) = \sigma_{c'}(\sigma_c(r))$.

results.title: Natural join
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The natural join $r \bowtie s$ of finite sets of tuples $r$ and $s$ is the set of merges of $t$ and $u$ over all pairs of tuples $t \in r$ and $u \in s$ that are compatible, that is, agree on every attribute where both are defined. The merge of $t$ and $u$ takes the value of $t$ where $t$ is defined and the value of $u$ otherwise.

results.title: Renaming of attributes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a permutation $f$ of the attributes and a finite set $r$ of tuples, the renaming $\rho_f(r)$ is the finite set of the tuples $t \circ f^{-1}$ for $t \in r$: each tuple keeps its values, and its value at an attribute $a$ moves to the attribute $f(a)$.

results.title: Commutativity of the natural join
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all finite sets $r$ and $s$ of tuples, $r \bowtie s = s \bowtie r$, where $\bowtie$ is the natural join.

results.title: Associativity of the natural join
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all finite sets $r$, $s$ and $w$ of tuples, $(r \bowtie s) \bowtie w = r \bowtie (s \bowtie w)$, where $\bowtie$ is the natural join.

results.title: The natural join on a common schema is the intersection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $r$ and $s$ are relations over the same schema $S$, that is, finite sets of tuples each over $S$, then their natural join is their intersection: $r \bowtie s = r \cap s$.

results.title: Selection distributes over union
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Assume the set of attributes is finite. Let $c$ be a selection condition and write $\sigma_c$ for selection by $c$. For finite sets $r$ and $s$ of tuples, $\sigma_c(r \cup s) = \sigma_c(r) \cup \sigma_c(s)$.

results.title: Selection distributes over difference
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Assume the set of attributes is finite. Let $c$ be a selection condition and write $\sigma_c$ for selection by $c$. For finite sets $r$ and $s$ of tuples, $\sigma_c(r \setminus s) = \sigma_c(r) \setminus \sigma_c(s)$.

results.title: Projection of a relation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite set $T$ of attributes and a finite set $r$ of tuples, the projection $\pi_T(r)$ is the finite set of the restrictions to $T$ of the tuples of $r$: $\pi_T(r) = \{ t|_T : t \in r \}$.

results.title: Membership in a join
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r$ be a relation over the schema $S$ and $s$ a relation over the schema $S'$, that is, finite sets of tuples each over $S$, respectively each over $S'$. A tuple $t$ belongs to the natural join $r \bowtie s$ if and only if $t$ is over $S \cup S'$, the restriction of $t$ to $S$ belongs to $r$, and the restriction of $t$ to $S'$ belongs to $s$.

results.title: Selection pushdown into the left operand of a join
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r$ be a relation over a schema $S$, that is, a finite set of tuples each defined exactly on the attributes of $S$, and let $s$ be any finite set of tuples. If every attribute of the selection condition $c$ lies in $S$, then $\sigma_c(r \bowtie s) = \sigma_c(r) \bowtie s$, where $\sigma_c$ is selection by $c$ and $\bowtie$ is the natural join.

results.title: Selection pushdown into the right operand of a join
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a relation over a schema $S'$, that is, a finite set of tuples each defined exactly on the attributes of $S'$, and let $r$ be any finite set of tuples. If every attribute of the selection condition $c$ lies in $S'$, then $\sigma_c(r \bowtie s) = r \bowtie \sigma_c(s)$, where $\sigma_c$ is selection by $c$ and $\bowtie$ is the natural join.

results.title: Cascade of projections
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Assume the set of attributes is finite. For all finite sets of attributes $T$ and $T'$ and every finite set $r$ of tuples, $\pi_T(\pi_{T'}(r)) = \pi_{T \cap T'}(r)$, where $\pi_T$ is projection onto $T$.

results.title: Cascade of projections onto a subset
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Assume the set of attributes is finite. For finite sets of attributes $T \subseteq T'$ and every finite set $r$ of tuples, $\pi_T(\pi_{T'}(r)) = \pi_T(r)$, where $\pi_T$ is projection onto $T$.

results.title: Selection commutes with projection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Assume the set of attributes is finite. Let $c$ be a selection condition, $T$ a finite set of attributes containing every attribute of $c$, and $r$ a finite set of tuples. Then $\sigma_c(\pi_T(r)) = \pi_T(\sigma_c(r))$, where $\sigma_c$ is selection by $c$ and $\pi_T$ is projection onto $T$.

results.title: Projection distributes over union
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite set $T$ of attributes and all finite sets $r$ and $s$ of tuples, the projection onto $T$ of $r \cup s$ is the union of the projections onto $T$ of $r$ and of $s$: $\pi_T(r \cup s) = \pi_T(r) \cup \pi_T(s)$.

results.title: Databases conforming to a schema
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $N$ be a set of relation names. A database schema assigns to each name $n \in N$ a finite set of attributes $\mathrm{sch}(n)$, and a database assigns to each name $n$ a finite set of tuples $\mathrm{db}(n)$. The database $\mathrm{db}$ conforms to the database schema $\mathrm{sch}$ when, for every name $n$, the set $\mathrm{db}(n)$ is a relation over $\mathrm{sch}(n)$.

results.title: Typing is sound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A well-formed query evaluates, on every conforming database, to a relation over its inferred schema.
